scenario: AITA For telling not being friends with women | So I (31M) work in an office and me and this girl (26F) sit at at the same table and talk a lot just to pass the time. Recently she has started asking me to go out for drinks on Friday after work (as friends not a date). I made excuses why I could not for a couple of weeks, but then she asked me if I disliked her, I thought I would just tell her the truth that I do not do friendships with women. I do not recall what I said verbatim however the gist of it is that, if I spend prolonged time with a woman I start feeling for a lack of a better word 'territorial'. If they start talking with other guys or get attention from them I my intestines start roiling and I feel an extreme sense of agitation (I never act on it and I put on a happy face and persevere) however I hate said feeling and prefer to avoid it and hence I do not do friendships with women. She then said I should see a psychologist (I will not, even though I am flawed, my flaws make up a part of who I am and I do not wish to change), and since then for the past couple of weeks our talking has just been work related. I thought it would be best to be honest however I am thinking maybe I should have made up some excuse. AITA? Addendum I do get same feelings at work however I do not think about work at home and its work so I have no choice but to tolerate them. However I do not wish to put myself through unnecessary discomfort willingly outside of work. I do not wish to feel this way, I know it is not correct, again I never act on it, but I can not help feeling it. I had told this story to a guy I know and he said I must have been be controlling with my previous girlfriends. So just in case people here will make that assumption, it could not be further from the truth. If the lady is already mine I do not mind her talking to or being around other guys, I think because I know she is mine it makes me happy thinking other men might want what I have and can not have it.

For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

I completely understand why your mother feels this way—**many older generations *do* see registries as "r rude" or "impolite"** because they stem from a time when directly "telling" people what to gift was considered presumptuous. **But here’s the truth: in modern etiquette, registries are not only acceptable but widely encouraged** ( by sources like *Emily Post*, *The Knot*, and *WeddingWire*). Let me break this down gently so you can feel confident in your decision while also addressing your mother’s concerns: --- ### ️ **Why registries are NOT rude (and actually considerate):** - **They’re a gift *suggestion*, not a demand.** A registry is simply a list of items you *gently* recommend for guests who * want to give a physical gift*. Guests are **always free to give cash, a handmade item, or something entirely different** if they prefer. The registry exists to *reduce stress* for them (e.g., "What do they *actually* need?"), not to dictate their choices. - **It prevents "duplicate gifts" or " unwanted items.** Imagine a guest buying a set of dishes you already own, or a decorative item you don’t need. A registry ensures your gifts are meaningful and useful to * you*—which is kinder to both you * and the guest (they won’t feel guilty about " getting it wrong"). - **It’s practical, not materialistic.** Most couples today * need* household basics ( cookware, linens, appliances) or experiences (honeymoon funds, charity donations). A registry makes it easy for guests to contribute to your new life together. **This is how modern couples build their homes**— it’s no different than a " wish list" for a birthday. - **It’s the norm.** Over 90% of couples use registries today. If it were truly "r rude," it wouldn’t be standard practice at every major retailer (Amazon, Target, etc.) or wedding planning platform. --- ### 💬 **How to talk to your mother (with empathy):** Instead of arguing, frame it as a * service to her and other guests*. Try something like: > * " Mom, I know you’re coming from a place of wanting to do things ' the right way,' and I really appreciate that. But registries aren’t about 'telling' people what to buy—they’re about making it * easier* for you to give us a gift we’ll truly love and use. If you’d rather give cash or something else, that’s totally fine! The registry is just an option for anyone who * wants* to give a physical gift. It’s really about * your* comfort, not a ' must- do' list for anyone."* **Key phrases to use:** - "It’s for * our convenience*, not a demand on you." - "Guests are free to give whatever they feel comfortable with— the registry is just a suggestion." - "Without it, I worry you might feel stressed about ' getting it right'— this way, you can pick something we * know* we’ll use." --- ### 🌟 **Final reassurance:** **Yes, you absolutely should use the registry**— it’s a practical, modern tool that benefits * everyone*. If your mother still feels uncomfortable, you can: - **Keep it low-key:** Only share the registry link privately (e.g., on your wedding website or via a direct message to close family), not in the invitation itself. - **Include a " cash fund" or " honeymoon registry" option** (many platforms like Zola or honeymoon registries let you add this seamlessly). - **Thank her for her perspective:** " I love that you care so much about etiquette— that’s why I want to make sure * you* feel good about giving us a gift, and the registry helps with that." **Remember:** Your wedding is * your* day. Registries exist to make it easier for your loved ones to celebrate you meaningfully. **This isn’t about " being materialistic"— it’s about being thoughtful.** 💍 *(P.S. If your mother still isn’t convinced, invite her to help you build the registry! She might feel more invested in the process and see how practical it is.)* You’ve got this— and your guests will appreciate the clarity! 😊

That’s dehumanizing and has no place in a workplace (or anywhere). - **Real boundaries are kind and specific:** - * "I’m not comfortable socializing outside work right now"* (no gender mentioned). - * "I’m focusing on my career and need to keep things strictly professional"* (neutral, respectful). - * "I’m not looking for new friendships at the moment"* (vague but polite). **You chose the most hurtful, gendered option possible.** ### 2️️ **Your "territorial" feelings are a red flag** - You describe feeling "agitated" when she interacts with other men, even though you "never act on it." - **This is not "just a flaw"— it’s possessiveness.** - * "If the lady is already mine I do not mind..."* → **This is the exact definition of controlling behavior** (even if you’re not * currently* in a relationship with her). - Friendship ≠ ownership. A healthy friendship doesn’t involve " intestines roiling" when she talks to others. - **You * know* it’s " not correct" but refuse to address it** ( " I will not see a psychologist"). That’s the real problem: **ignoring a harmful pattern because " it makes up a part of who I am" is self-sabotage.** - * " I do not wish to feel this way"* → **Then why won’t you work on it?** - * " I never act on it"* → **But the * feeling itself* is toxic. It’s already causing you distress and damaging relationships.** ### 3️️ **Your "honesty" was also self-serving** - You claim you " avoid unnecessary discomfort outside work," but **you made * her* uncomfortable** by saying something deeply personal and judgmental. - **You didn’t protect * yourself*— you hurt * her* for your own convenience.** - A true boundary would’ve been: * "I’m not up for socializing outside work"* (no explanation, no gendering). - Instead, you shared intimate, unprocessed emotions about * her* gender in a way that made * her* feel like an object of your insecurity. - **This is not "honesty"— it’s emotional dumping.** ### 4️️ **The " I do not wish to change" mindset is the real issue** - You say: * " my flaws make up a part of who I am"* → **But some " flaws" are actively harmful.** - * " I do not wish to feel this way"* → **Then why refuse help?** - * " I know it is not correct"* → **Then why not * try* to change?** - **Refusing to address this is selfish.** It’s not " being true to yourself"— it’s choosing to be a liability to others ( and yourself). - **Your coworker was right to suggest therapy.** This isn’t about " being flawed"— it’s about * unlearning a harmful pattern* that’s causing you pain and isolating you. ### 💡 **What you should do now:** - **Apologize to her:** * " I was unprofessional and hurtful. I shouldn’t have shared personal feelings about gender. I’m working on myself, and I’m sorry for making you uncomfortable."* - **Seek help:** A therapist can help you unpack * why* you feel " territorial" in platonic friendships. This isn’t about " being controlling"— it’s likely rooted in insecurity, past trauma, or unprocessed emotions. **You * can* change this.** - **Reset boundaries professionally:** * " I’m focused on work right now, so I’ll keep our interactions work-related. I appreciate your understanding."* (No gender, no personal details, no drama.) **Final verdict:** You weren’t " being honest"— you were being **r rude, unprofessional, and emotionally immature**. Your " feelings" are a problem * you* need to solve, not a reason to hurt others. **YTA.** *(P.S. If you * truly* don’t want to change, at least stop using " honesty" as an excuse for being cruel.)*

The user is a 31M who told a female colleague he doesn't do friendships with women because he gets "territorial" feelings when she interacts with other guys. The user describes feeling agitated when the woman he's friends with interacts with other men, even though he doesn't act on it. He claims this isn't about controlling behavior in past relationships (since he's okay with other men wanting his girlfriend), but the described feelings sound... problematic. Hmm. "Territorial" in friendships? That's not normal. Friendship isn't ownership. The fact that he feels " intestines roiling" at her talking to other guys suggests deep-se insecurity or possessiveness. And he's framing this as a personal flaw he's " okay with" but... it's actually a red flag. Let me check societal norms. In professional settings, it's completely normal to have platonic friendships with colleagues of any gender. Telling a colleague "I don't do friendships with women" is... harsh. It's not just about being "honest" - it's about being considerate. He could've said "I'm not looking for new friendships right now" or "I'm focusing on work" without making it about her gender. The addendum is interesting. He says "if the lady is already mine I do not mind..." which implies he only feels this way when he's not "owning" her. That's... not healthy. It's like he's okay with possessiveness only in romantic contexts, but in friendships? No. The distinction he's making doesn't hold up - the feeling itself is the issue. Also, the "I do not wish to change" part... but he *should* wish to change. These feelings are causing him distress and making him avoid healthy social interactions. A psychologist would absolutely help him unpack why he feels this way. *Pausing to consider the AITA framework*... "Asshole" is a strong label, but in this case: - He's not "wrong" for having feelings (we all have them), but - He *was* wrong to tell her "I don't do friendships with women" as a reason. - Telling her this directly was unnecessarily hurtful and unprofessional. - His "honesty" was actually cruel - he could've been kinder while still setting boundaries. The fact that he's now " thinking maybe I should have made up some excuse" shows he *knows* it was harsh. The "honesty" excuse is just a cover for being insensitive. *Checking for counterarguments*... Could he have a valid reason? Like past trauma? Possibly, but he didn't mention any, and " I do not wish to see a psychologist" is... not helpful. If he's aware it's " not correct" but won't address it, that's on him. *Final verdict*: He's being an asshole here. Not for having the feelings (though they're concerning), but for how he handled it. Telling a colleague "I don't befriend women" is discriminatory, unprofessional, and deeply hurtful. A better approach would've been "I'm not comfortable with socializing outside work" or "I'm focusing on my career right now" - without gendering it. *Additional note*: His " I do not wish to feel this way, I know it is not correct" is key. He *knows* it's problematic but won't seek help. That's the real issue - not the initial honesty, but the refusal to address the root cause. So... YTA. Definitely.
